title: Rahab (Joshua 2)
hook: a woman on the city wall hides the spies and asks for her family's safety; the rabbis count her among the great converts

segments.voice: Yesterday, be strong, three times to Joshua and once back from the people. Your line was be strong, again. Today, two spies, and the woman who saves them.

Night, in Jericho. A knock at a door in the city wall: the king's men. Two strangers were seen coming into this house, they say. Bring them out. Upstairs, on the flat roof, two men lie very still under stalks of flax laid out to dry. The woman of the house is called Rahab. What she says in the next minute decides whether those men live. She's not from their people. She owes them nothing. And she's about to bet her own family on them.
screen: `A KNOCK IN THE CITY WALL.` → `TWO SPIES UNDER THE FLAX.` → `RAHAB DECIDES.`

segments.voice: She tells the soldiers: yes, men came, but they left at dusk, before the gate closed. Go after them quickly and you'll catch them. The soldiers run off toward the river. Then she climbs to the roof, and she talks. We've heard what your God did, she says, how the sea dried up in front of you. Our hearts melted. And then, from a stranger, a sentence of faith: the Lord your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below. Then she bargains. I was kind to you; swear to be kind to my father's house: my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and everyone who belongs to them. The spies swear. Her house is built into the wall itself, so she lets them down by a rope through her window. They leave her a sign: tie "this line of scarlet thread" in that window, gather your family inside, and whoever is in the house will be safe. The Hebrew calls her a zonah, a harlot. The ancient Aramaic translation, and Rashi after it, read the word as an innkeeper, a woman who sold food; other readers keep the plain sense. Either way, she lives at the edge of the city, and she's the one who sees clearly. The Talmud remembers that she converted and joined Israel, and tells that prophets came from her line. And the Hebrew word for that red cord is tikvah, the same word Hebrew uses for hope.
screen: `SHE SENDS THE SOLDIERS AWAY.` · `GOD IN HEAVEN AND ON EARTH.` · `SAVE MY WHOLE FAMILY.` · then, large: `THE SCARLET CORD.` · then: `TIKVAH: A CORD, A HOPE.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is exposed right now: someone sick, someone new and alone, someone being talked about, someone who can't speak up for themselves. Hold them a moment, by name if you can, and ask what a scarlet cord would be for them: a message, a meal, a word in their favor when they're not in the room, a door you could open. Then sit with them in mind.
Rahab. The woman on the wall of Jericho who hid the spies, bargained for her family, and tied a scarlet cord in her window. Today's word.
Your line: the scarlet cord. One woman on the wall saw clearly, and saved her whole family. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read Joshua 2 as the haftarah for the Torah portion Shelach, the story of the earlier spies, and the Talmud remembers Rahab as a convert who joined the people of Israel.

chat.says: Why does the Bible make a hero of Rahab? She wasn't even an Israelite.
options: She hid the spies, spoke faith in their God, and the Talmud says she converted.
She was secretly an Israelite all along, hiding inside Jericho's walls.
She only helped because the spies paid her; faith never came into it.
chat.meaning: Rahab risks her life for the spies and says their God is God in heaven and on earth; the Talmud remembers her conversion.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording 'this line of scarlet thread' (Joshua 2:18).
Targum Jonathan renders zonah as pundekita (innkeeper) and Rashi follows; confirm. Both readings given without ranking.

'Rabbinic tradition remembers her as one of the great converts' follows the outline's hook; confirm the sources (e.g., Mekhilta, Megillah 14b) and wording. The Talmud's tradition that prophets descended from her (Megillah 14b) is given without names or numbers.
Tikvah as both 'cord' and 'hope' is a lexical observation framed as 'some readers notice'; a Keeper may cut it under the strict claims rule.
Rahab's false trail to the soldiers is told without moral comment; a Keeper may want to note rabbinic discussion of it.
